title: Neural Cell Types
intro: A brain is not built from one kind of neuron. Pyramidal cells, fast-spiking basket cells, Purkinje cells, thalamic relay cells and dozens of others differ in shape, in the ion channels they carry, in whom they talk to and in how they fire. This section walks through the cell types that matter most for building spiking models, and for each one says what computational models of it exist, from detailed multi-compartment reconstructions down to two-variable point neurons.

blocks.text: Why cell types matter for a model builder

Most spiking networks use one neuron model with one parameter set. Real circuits get much of their computing power from having several kinds of cell that play different roles: excitatory cells that carry information, fast inhibitory cells that set timing and enforce sparseness, dendrite-targeting cells that gate feedback, pacemakers that set rhythms, and huge integrating cells that read out learned associations. Knowing the types tells you which roles your model is missing, and the existing models of each type give you parameter sets you can start from instead of tuning from scratch.

items: Defining a Cell Type (#/neuroscience/cell-types/classification): the four ways neuroscientists sort neurons (shape, firing, genes, connections) and the large atlases that combine them.
Modelling a Cell Type (#/neuroscience/cell-types/modelling-cell-types): the ladder of model detail, how models are fitted to recordings, and where to download published models.
Firing Patterns (#/neuroscience/cell-types/firing-patterns): the electrophysiological classes (regular spiking, bursting, fast spiking and so on) with an interactive Izhikevich neuron.
Cortical Excitatory Neurons (#/neuroscience/cell-types/cortical-excitatory): layer 2/3, layer 4, layer 5 and layer 6 principal cells.
Cortical Interneurons (#/neuroscience/cell-types/cortical-interneurons): PV basket, chandelier, SST Martinotti, VIP and neurogliaform cells.
Hippocampal and Entorhinal Neurons (#/neuroscience/cell-types/hippocampal): CA1 and CA3 pyramidal cells, dentate granule cells, OLM interneurons and entorhinal stellate cells.
Cerebellar Neurons (#/neuroscience/cell-types/cerebellar): Purkinje cells, granule cells and inferior olive neurons.
Thalamic Neurons (#/neuroscience/cell-types/thalamic): thalamocortical relay cells and thalamic reticular cells.
Basal Ganglia and Neuromodulatory Neurons (#/neuroscience/cell-types/basal-ganglia-and-neuromodulatory): striatal medium spiny neurons, dopamine neurons and fast-spiking striatal interneurons.
Sensory and Motor Neurons (#/neuroscience/cell-types/sensory-and-motor): retinal cells and spinal motor neurons, the brain's input and output ends.
Glial Cells (#/neuroscience/cell-types/glia): astrocytes, oligodendrocytes and microglia, which are not neurons but change what neurons compute.

blocks.text: E = excitatory (glutamatergic), I = inhibitory (GABAergic), mod = neuromodulatory. Purkinje cells are inhibitory projection neurons: their GABAergic output leaves the cerebellar cortex. Medium spiny neurons are also GABAergic projection neurons.
What a cortical column model needs first

If your goal is a spiking cortical column, the cortical pages come first: pyramidal cells per layer and the three main interneuron classes (PV, SST, VIP). The thalamic page matters next, because the column's main input and one of its output loops run through the thalamus. Hippocampal and entorhinal cells are where grid and place codes, the location signal behind the Thousand Brains Theory, were found. The cerebellum and basal ganglia are worth reading for contrast: they show that very different cell types solve very different learning problems (supervised error correction and reinforcement learning).

The shorter Cell Types page in the learning path (#/computational-cortical-columns/neocortex-biology/cell-types) gives the minimum cortical summary and connectivity motifs; the pages here go deeper into each type and its models.
